disputing claims made by Davis in his memoir The Soundtrack of My Life. Davis had written that Clarkson cried
hysterically in his office after being pressured to record "Since U Been Gone". Clarkson countered that she became
emotional not over that song, but in response to remarks Davis allegedly made about her songwriting on "Because of
You", including criticism that its lyrics did not rhyme and suggesting that she "should just shut up and sing". She also
criticized Davis for omitting his role in blaming the underperformance of My December on its lack of radio-friendly
singles and her involvement in its songwriting.
Clarkson has stated that there have been several instances throughout her career where she declined songwriting
credit on songs, despite making changes to them. However, she noted that she will typically request credit if she
believes her contributions warrant it. In 2017, Clarkson said that she refused songwriting credit on "My Life Would Suck
Without You", one of her biggest hits, as a form of protest against being forced by her record label to work with
producer Dr. Luke after expressing that she had not enjoyed working with him prior. She has suggested that by doing
so, she may have forfeited millions of dollars in potential royalties, but maintains that she is against recording artists
stealing credit from professional songwriters.
Influences
At age eight, Clarkson was first inspired to venture into music during a visit to an <color=#3366CC>African-American church</color> in <color=#3366CC>Fort</color>
<color=#3366CC>Worth, Texas</color>. She recalled: "I was like, 'Wow, whatever they're feeling, I want to feel it too'." Clarkson has been
influenced by musicians across various genres. She cited soul singer <color=#3366CC>Aretha Franklin</color> as her major influence. Many of
her chosen Idol numbers were Aretha Franklin covers, including "(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman", which is
considered her breakout moment during the competition. Other soul acts who influenced Clarkson were <color=#3366CC>Whitney</color>

<color=#3366CC>Houston</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mariah Carey</color>, <color=#3366CC>Etta James</color> and <color=#3366CC>Stevie Wonder</color>. Clarkson was also influenced by <color=#3366CC>Christina Aguilera</color>, by rock
acts such as <color=#3366CC>Radiohead</color>, Garbage, <color=#3366CC>Aerosmith</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Jimi Hendrix</color>, as well as Reba McEntire, <color=#3366CC>Bette Midler</color>, and
Rosemary Clooney. Regarding her musical influence, Clarkson explained:
I grew up with three totally different parents that were into different music. My stepfather is into <color=#3366CC>Willie Nelson</color> and <color=#3366CC>Elvis</color>
and all that kind of stuff. And my real father is into Whitney and Mariah, and Aretha, all those soulful singers. My mom
is into more, like, adult contemporary—<color=#3366CC>Celine Dion</color>, <color=#3366CC>Barbra [Streisand]</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bette Midler</color>, all those types of things. And then
my brother is a big influence on me. He's like ten years older than me, so you always wanna be around your cool
brother and hang out, so I grew up loving <color=#3366CC>Guns N' Roses</color>. I was all about <color=#3366CC>Metallica</color>. I was all about all those bands, and
I still am. I love <color=#3366CC>Aerosmith</color> and No Doubt. I have so many influences on me that are so different. And even country. I
love Reba McEntire. I could listen to her all the time. In 2006, Clarkson said she does not consider herself to be a pop
singer, explaining, "Rock is what I love". Clarkson often covers rock songs on her Kellyoke segment of her talk show,
such as Metallica's "Sad but True", and Heart's "Crazy on You".
Musical style

Although Clarkson's music primarily incorporates <color=#3366CC>pop</color>, her discography also spans <color=#3366CC>rock</color>, <color=#3366CC>country</color>, and <color=#3366CC>R&B</color>. Her style
has been described as <color=#3366CC>pop rock</color>, <color=#3366CC>pop-punk</color>, and power pop.
Impact
Clarkson has scored over 100 number ones on the Billboard charts and has a star on the <color=#3366CC>Hollywood Walk of Fame</color>.
Clarkson has sold over 25 million albums and 45 million singles worldwide, including 14 million albums and 35 million
digital singles in the United States alone. She became the first artist to top each of Billboards pop, adult contemporary,
country and dance charts. She was ranked nineteenth on VH1's list of 100 Greatest Women in Music. Television
channel Fuse included Clarkson among "30 Greatest Musicians to Come From Singing Competitions" list. <color=#3366CC>Rolling</color>
<color=#3366CC>Stone</color> ranked her 194 on their list of 200 Best Singers of All Time in 2023. In 2025, Billboard ranked Clarkson at
number 11 on its "Top 100 Women Artists of the 21st Century" list.
Music executive <color=#3366CC>Simon Cowell</color> believed that "What [Clarkson] sold in the UK, Europe, Asia had nothing to do with
American Idol. It had everything to do with the fact that she made a great record and she's got an incredible voice.
She's not a girl who got lucky in a talent competition; we got lucky to find her." According to <color=#3366CC>The Hollywood Reporter</color>,
Clarkson is "the embodiment of the perfect pop star. Her unmistakable pipes are a powerful presence in top 40 and
country, with forays into anthemic rock and dance." Nolan Feeney from <color=#3366CC>Time</color> asserted that Clarkson "has had more of a
lasting impact on the pop music landscape than casual listeners might realize."
According to Billboard, Clarkson was a "phenomenon" who "helped legitimize" the impact of talent shows. <color=#3366CC>The</color>
<color=#3366CC>Washington Post</color> wrote that "Clarkson's powerhouse voice and dynamic presence signaled that the music industry
should take these reality show contestants seriously: Her first two albums, Thankful and Breakaway, sold about ten
million copies combined, and her pop tunes became empowerment anthems across the globe." In 2007, journalist
Nekesa Mumbi Moody reported that the success of Breakaway in particular was the true pivotal moment in establishing
American Idols credibility, proving that the show was capable of "finding someone who would have a career with
longevity". Glenn Gamboa of Newsday believed Clarkson "has set the standard for all singing competition contestants
with her savvy mix of pop, rock and country." <color=#3366CC>Fox Broadcasting Company</color> said that Clarkson gave "lasting credibility" to
American Idol and "in so many ways she cleared a road" for all of the next contestants. George Varga from The San
Diego Union-Tribune underlined the difference of Clarkson from most other talent show contestants is that she "writes
or co-writes a fair number of [her] own songs. She is also the only one whose quest to follow her artistic instincts—the
better to rock out and break free from the Idol cookie-cutter pop mold—prompted her to fire her management team and
engage in a prolonged public battle with her record company, RCA."
Jon Lisi from PopMatters named Clarkson as one of the forces of female domination in pop music of the 2000s. He
explained that "Clarkson's anti-sexual image appealed to those who were uncomfortable with <color=#3366CC>Britney Spears</color>' overt
exhibitionism. When Clarkson performed 'Since U Been Gone' at the 2005 MTV Video Music Awards, for instance, she
only showed her midriff, and it was clear that she was marketing herself to an alternative group of young females who
liked pop music's conventional sound but didn't want to be confronted with sexual imagery." Mickey Rapkin of <color=#3366CC>Billboard</color>
magazine, who called Clarkson a role model and compared her vocals to golden-era Aretha Franklin, stated that
Clarkson "has never shied away from speaking her mind, whether in her propulsive pop anthems or on her filter-free
Twitter feed." Clarkson has influenced other artists including Vanessa Hudgens, Demi Lovato, Ava Max, Jordin Sparks,
Ashley Tisdale, <color=#3366CC>Avril Lavigne</color>, Kelsea Ballerini, and Priscilla Block.
Personal life
In February 2012, Clarkson began dating talent manager Brandon Blackstock, son of her former manager Narvel
Blackstock and former stepson of Reba McEntire; Blackstock was married to another woman at the time. She married
Blackstock on October 20, 2013, at Blackberry Farm in Walland, Tennessee. During their marriage, Brandon was her
manager. They had two children, a daughter born June 12, 2014, and a son born April 12, 2016. In June 2020,
Clarkson filed for divorce from Blackstock, citing irreconcilable differences. In March 2022, it was reported their divorce
had been finalized. On November 21, 2023, Clarkson was awarded more than $2.6 million from Blackstock for
commissions paid to him for business deals he procured as her manager. The California Labor Commissioner ruled
that Blackstock violated the state's Talent Agencies Act by handling these deals, which should have been managed by
Clarkson's talent agents at Creative Artists Agency. The ruling included commissions from Clarkson's role on The Voice
and other promotional agreements, but did not require repayment for deals related to The Kelly Clarkson Show.
Blackstock died of <color=#3366CC>melanoma</color> on August 7, 2025, aged 48.
In October 2019, Clarkson said that she has been managing an autoimmune condition and a <color=#3366CC>thyroid</color> condition since
2006, which she had previously addressed on <color=#3366CC>Today</color> in 2018.
In February 2022, Clarkson changed her legal name to Kelly Brianne. In an interview, she said she did so due to a
strained relationship with her late father, but that her professional name would not change.
Political views
In 2011, Clarkson said, "I am a <color=#3366CC>Republican</color> but I actually voted <color=#3366CC>Democrat</color> last election", and expressed support for Ron
Paul. Clarkson later said she would vote for <color=#3366CC>Barack Obama</color> in the 2012 United States presidential election, telling the
Daily Star, "I can't support <color=#3366CC>Romney</color>'s policies as I have a lot of gay friends and I don't think it's fair they can't get
married." She added, "I'm not a hardcore feminist but we can't be going back to the '50s."
In the 2016 United States presidential election, Clarkson endorsed <color=#3366CC>Hillary Clinton</color> and said that <color=#3366CC>Donald Trump</color> made
her "genuinely frightened for our nation". In 2017, Clarkson said she is a Democrat.
Philanthropy
In April 2007, Clarkson took part in "Idol Gives Back", a fundraiser for people in poverty in Africa and the U.S.,
performing "Up to the Mountain" with <color=#3366CC>Jeff Beck</color>. She also performed a five-song set later that year on the American leg
of Live Earth concerts promoting environmental awareness about climate change. She has served as ambassador for
the March of Dimes since she was on American Idol, raising money regularly and assisting in volunteer service, having
walked for "March for Babies" for the cause of improvement of the health of mothers and babies. Clarkson also got
involved in the organization Houses of Hope, which builds orphanages for children in <color=#3366CC>South Africa</color> affected by
<color=#3366CC>HIV/AIDS</color>, abuse, and poverty. She has visited those children and also participated in "A Night for Hope" fund-raiser
concert (held by Clarkson's background vocal singers, Jill and Kate), performing a song she wrote after her trip to
South Africa, "You Still Won't Know What It's Like". Clarkson also supports the charities Save the Children, <color=#3366CC>UNICEF</color>,
"Do Something" and "STOMP Out Bullying", and music causes like the Save the Music Foundation.
Clarkson had a ranch in Texas for unwanted animals, which included amputee goats, blind dogs, and horses that
survived colic; there are more than 80 animals at the sanctuary. She helped provide veterinary care for them and found
them an adoptive family. On March 1, 2013, she performed in a benefit concert supporting the <color=#3366CC>Omaha</color>-based
Opportunity Education Foundation, which provides access to education for children around the world, saying,
"Education was a key part of my childhood, and I am better for it. Anything for education I am really into and especially
for kids. A lot of people don't have computers, and they can't afford them. Without education, you get far behind. As
long as they have a chance, you know, I think that's important. I want every kid to have a chance." In 2013, Clarkson
teamed with State Farm Insurance to support teen safe driving as a part of Celebrate My Drive program, and supported
Feeding America and The Ad Council and its Child Hunger PSA Campaign, which provides food for children facing
hunger. Also in 2013, she participated in Green Mountain Coffee's Great Coffee, Good Vibes, Choose Fair Trade
campaign, traveling to coffee farms in Peru to draw attention to the importance of Fair Trade certification.

Written works
Human
Humans (Homo sapiens, meaning 'thinking man' or 'wise man') are the most abundant and widespread <color=#3366CC>species</color> of
<color=#3366CC>primates</color>, characterized by <color=#3366CC>bipedalism</color>, minimal body hair, and large, complex brains enabling the development of

advanced <color=#3366CC>technology</color>, <color=#3366CC>culture</color>, and <color=#3366CC>language</color>. Humans are highly social beings and tend to live in complex <color=#3366CC>social</color>

<color=#3366CC>structures</color> composed of many cooperating and competing groups, from <color=#3366CC>families</color> and <color=#3366CC>kinship</color> networks to political <color=#3366CC>states</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Social interactions</color> between humans have established a wide variety of values, <color=#3366CC>social norms</color>, and <color=#3366CC>rituals</color>, which bolster
human <color=#3366CC>society</color>. <color=#3366CC>Curiosity</color> and the human desire to understand and influence the environment have motivated
humanity's development of <color=#3366CC>science</color>, <color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, <color=#3366CC>religion</color>, <color=#3366CC>mythology</color>, and other fields of knowledge.
Humans have a large and highly developed prefrontal cortex, the region of the brain associated with higher <color=#3366CC>cognition</color>.
They are intelligent beings, capable of episodic memory, flexible <color=#3366CC>facial expressions</color>, self-awareness and a <color=#3366CC>theory of</color>

<color=#3366CC>mind</color>. The human mind is capable of <color=#3366CC>introspection</color> (metacognition), private <color=#3366CC>thought</color>, <color=#3366CC>imagination</color>, volition, and forming
views on <color=#3366CC>existence</color>. Humans can also mentally travel through time (chronesthesia), which signifies episodic foresight.
These attributes have allowed them to achieve large technological advancements through <color=#3366CC>reason</color> and the transmission
of knowledge to future generations. In <color=#3366CC>cultural anthropology</color>, the cumulative preservation and advancement of
knowledge across generations is known as the ratchet effect.
Humans are <color=#3366CC>omnivorous</color>, capable of consuming a wide variety of plant and animal material, and have <color=#3366CC>used fire</color> to
prepare and <color=#3366CC>cook</color> food. They can survive for up to eight weeks without food, and three or four days without water.
Humans are generally diurnal, sleeping on average seven to nine hours per day. Human <color=#3366CC>childbirth</color> is dangerous, with a
high risk of complications and death. Both the mother and the father typically provide care for human offspring, who are
helpless at birth.

<color=#3366CC>Genes</color> and the <color=#3366CC>environment</color> influence <color=#3366CC>human biological variation</color> in appearance, <color=#3366CC>physiology</color>, <color=#3366CC>immune system</color>, <color=#3366CC>mental</color>
<color=#3366CC>abilities</color>, body size, and <color=#3366CC>lifespan</color>. Though humans vary in many traits, any two humans are on average over 99%
genetically similar, with the most genetically diverse populations from <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>. The greatest degree of genetic variation
exists between males and females. On average, males have greater body strength and females generally have a
higher <color=#3366CC>body fat</color> percentage. Females undergo <color=#3366CC>menopause</color> and become <color=#3366CC>infertile</color> potentially decades before the end of
their lives. They also have a <color=#3366CC>longer life span</color> in almost every population around the world. The division into male and
female <color=#3366CC>gender roles</color> has varied historically, and challenges to predominant gender norms have recurred in many
societies.
<color=#3366CC>Humans evolved</color> from other <color=#3366CC>hominins</color> in Africa several million years ago. Although some scientists equate humans with
all members of the genus <color=#3366CC>Homo</color>, in common usage it generally refers to Homo sapiens, the only extant member. Homo
sapiens <color=#3366CC>emerged</color> around 300,000 years ago and migrated <color=#3366CC>out of Africa</color>, gradually replacing local populations of <color=#3366CC>archaic</color>
<color=#3366CC>humans</color>. Early humans were <color=#3366CC>hunter-gatherers</color>, before the <color=#3366CC>invention of agriculture</color> and domestication of animals led to
permanent settlement in the <color=#3366CC>Fertile Crescent</color> and other <color=#3366CC>cradles of civilization</color>. As food surpluses enabled populations to

become <color=#3366CC>larger</color> and <color=#3366CC>denser</color>, forms of <color=#3366CC>governance</color> developed, the use of <color=#3366CC>writing</color> became necessary, and a number of
<color=#3366CC>civilizations</color> rose and fell. Humans have continued to expand, with over 8.3 billion humans occupying almost all regions
of Earth in 2026, and have even <color=#3366CC>visited the Moon</color>. This expansion, combined with <color=#3366CC>industrialization</color>, has led to
<color=#3366CC>environmental destruction</color> and <color=#3366CC>pollution</color> that significantly contributes to the ongoing <color=#3366CC>mass extinction</color> of many other
forms of life.
Etymology and definition
All modern humans are classified into the <color=#3366CC>species</color> Homo sapiens, coined by <color=#3366CC>Carl Linnaeus</color> in his 1735 work Systema
Naturae. The <color=#3366CC>generic</color> name <color=#3366CC>Homo</color> is a learned 18th-century derivation from Latin homō, which refers to humans of
either sex. The word human can refer to all members of the Homo genus. The name Homo sapiens means 'wise man'
or 'knowledgeable man'. There is <color=#3366CC>disagreement</color> about whether certain extinct members of the genus, namely
<color=#3366CC>Neanderthals</color>, should be included as a separate species of humans or as a <color=#3366CC>subspecies</color> of H. sapiens.

Human is a <color=#3366CC>loanword</color> of <color=#3366CC>Middle English</color> from <color=#3366CC>Old French</color> humain, ultimately from <color=#3366CC>Latin</color> hūmānus, the adjectival form of
homō ('man' – in the sense of humanity). The native English term man can refer to the species generally (a synonym
for humanity) as well as to human males. It may also refer to individuals of either sex.
Although the word animal is colloquially used as an antonym for human, and contrary to a common biological
misconception, humans are <color=#3366CC>animals</color>. The word <color=#3366CC>person</color> is often used interchangeably with human, but philosophical
debate exists as to whether personhood applies to all humans or all <color=#3366CC>sentient beings</color>, and further if a human can lose
personhood (such as by going into a <color=#3366CC>persistent vegetative state</color>) and what the beginning of human personhood is.
Evolution
Humans belong to the biological <color=#3366CC>family</color> of great apes (family <color=#3366CC>Hominidae</color>, <color=#3366CC>superfamily Hominoidea</color>). The lineage of apes
that eventually gave rise to humans first split from <color=#3366CC>gibbons</color> (family Hylobatidae), next <color=#3366CC>orangutans</color> (genus Pongo), then

<color=#3366CC>gorillas</color> (genus Gorilla), and finally, <color=#3366CC>chimpanzees</color> and <color=#3366CC>bonobos</color> (genus <color=#3366CC>Pan</color>). The last split, between the human and
chimpanzee–bonobo lineages, took place around 8–4 million years ago, in the late <color=#3366CC>Miocene</color> epoch. During this split,
chromosome 2 was formed in humans from the joining of two other chromosomes, leaving humans with only 23 pairs of
chromosomes, compared to 24 for the other apes. Following their split with chimpanzees and bonobos, the <color=#3366CC>hominins</color>
diversified into many species and at least two distinct genera. All but one of these lineages – representing the genus
<color=#3366CC>Homo</color> and its sole extant species Homo sapiens – are now extinct.
The genus Homo evolved from <color=#3366CC>Australopithecus</color>. Though fossils from the transition are scarce, the earliest members of
Homo share several key traits with Australopithecus. Due to the scant available evidence, the time of the divergence to
the genus Homo does not have a consensus. Some studies using molecular clock techniques estimate the Homo
genus appeared 4.30–2.56 million years ago, while others contest that some early Homo species are incorrectly
included in the genus and therefore put this estimate at about 1.87 million years ago.
The earliest record of Homo is the 2.8 million-year-old specimen LD 350-1 from <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia</color>, and the earliest named
species are <color=#3366CC>Homo habilis</color> and <color=#3366CC>Homo rudolfensis</color>, which evolved by 2.3 million years ago. <color=#3366CC>H. erectus</color> (the African variant
is sometimes called <color=#3366CC>H. ergaster</color>) evolved 2 million years ago and was the first <color=#3366CC>archaic human</color> species to leave Africa
and disperse across Eurasia. H. erectus also was the first to evolve a characteristically human body plan. Homo
sapiens emerged in Africa at least 300,000 years ago from a species commonly designated as either <color=#3366CC>H.</color>
<color=#3366CC>heidelbergensis</color> or <color=#3366CC>H. rhodesiensis</color>, the descendants of H. erectus that remained in Africa. H. sapiens migrated out of
the continent, gradually replacing or interbreeding with local populations of archaic humans. Humans began exhibiting
<color=#3366CC>behavioral modernity</color> about 160,000–70,000 years ago, and possibly earlier. This development was likely selected
amidst <color=#3366CC>natural climate change</color> in Middle to Late Pleistocene Africa.
The <color=#3366CC>"out of Africa" migration</color> took place in at least two waves, the first around 130,000 to 100,000 years ago, the
second (Southern Dispersal) around 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. H. sapiens proceeded to colonize all the continents
and larger islands except Antarctica, arriving in <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> 125,000 years ago, Australia around 65,000 years ago, the

Americas around 15,000 years ago, and remote islands such as <color=#3366CC>Hawaii</color>, <color=#3366CC>Easter Island</color>, <color=#3366CC>Madagascar</color>, and <color=#3366CC>New Zealand</color>
in the years 300 to 1280 CE.
Human evolution was not a simple linear or branched progression but involved <color=#3366CC>interbreeding between related species</color>.
Genomic research has shown that hybridization between substantially diverged lineages was common in human
evolution. <color=#3366CC>DNA</color> evidence suggests that several genes of Neanderthal origin are present among all non
sub-Saharan-African populations, and Neanderthals and other hominins, such as <color=#3366CC>Denisovans</color>, may have contributed up
to 6% of their <color=#3366CC>genome</color> to present-day non sub-Saharan-African humans.

Human evolution is characterized by a number of <color=#3366CC>morphological</color>, <color=#3366CC>developmental</color>, <color=#3366CC>physiological</color>, and <color=#3366CC>behavioral</color> changes
that have taken place since the split between the last common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees. The most
significant of these adaptations are hairlessness, obligate bipedalism, increased brain size, and decreased <color=#3366CC>sexual</color>
<color=#3366CC>dimorphism</color> (neoteny). The relationship between all these changes is the subject of ongoing debate.
History
Prehistory
Until about 12,000 years ago, all humans lived as <color=#3366CC>hunter-gatherers</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Neolithic Revolution</color> (the invention of
<color=#3366CC>agriculture</color>) first took place in <color=#3366CC>Southwest Asia</color> and spread through large parts of the <color=#3366CC>Old World</color> over the following
millennia. It also occurred independently in <color=#3366CC>Mesoamerica</color> (about 6,000 years ago), China, <color=#3366CC>Papua New Guinea</color>, and the
<color=#3366CC>Sahel</color> and <color=#3366CC>West Savanna</color> regions of Africa.
The formation of permanent <color=#3366CC>human settlements</color>, the <color=#3366CC>domestication</color> of animals, and the <color=#3366CC>use of metal tools</color> were followed
by a permanent food surplus, for the first time in history. Agriculture and a sedentary lifestyle led to the emergence of
early civilizations.
Ancient
An urban revolution took place in the 4th millennium BCE with the development of <color=#3366CC>city-states</color>, particularly <color=#3366CC>Sumerian</color>
cities located in <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color>. It was in these cities that the earliest known form of writing, <color=#3366CC>cuneiform script</color>, appeared
around 3000 BCE. Other major civilizations to develop around this time were <color=#3366CC>Ancient Egypt</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley</color>
<color=#3366CC>Civilization</color>. They eventually traded with each other and invented technology such as wheels, plows and sails.
Emerging by 3000 BCE, the <color=#3366CC>Caral–Supe civilization</color> is the oldest complex civilization in the Americas. Astronomy and
mathematics were also developed, and the <color=#3366CC>Great Pyramid of Giza</color> was built. There is evidence of a severe drought
lasting about a hundred years that may have caused the decline of these civilizations, with new ones appearing in the
aftermath. <color=#3366CC>Babylonians</color> came to dominate Mesopotamia while others—such as the Poverty Point culture, <color=#3366CC>Minoans</color>, and
the <color=#3366CC>Shang dynasty</color>—rose to prominence in new areas. The <color=#3366CC>Late Bronze Age collapse</color> around 1200 BCE resulted in the
disappearance of a number of civilizations and the beginning of the <color=#3366CC>Greek Dark Ages</color>. During this period iron started
replacing bronze, leading to the <color=#3366CC>Iron Age</color>.
In the 5th century BCE, history started being <color=#3366CC>recorded as a discipline</color>, which provided a much clearer picture of life at
the time. Between the 8th and 6th centuries BCE, Europe entered the <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color> age, a period when <color=#3366CC>ancient</color>
<color=#3366CC>Greece</color> and <color=#3366CC>ancient Rome</color> flourished. Around this time, other civilizations also came to prominence. The <color=#3366CC>Maya</color>
<color=#3366CC>civilization</color> started to build cities and create complex calendars. In Africa, the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Aksum</color> overtook the declining
<color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Kush</color> and facilitated trade between India and the Mediterranean. In West Asia, the <color=#3366CC>Achaemenid Empire</color>'s
system of centralized governance became the precursor to many later empires, while the <color=#3366CC>Gupta Empire</color> in India and
the <color=#3366CC>Han dynasty</color> in China have been described as golden ages in their respective regions.
Post-classical
Following the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color> in 476, Europe entered the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>. During this period,
<color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Church</color> would act as a source of authority and education. In the Middle East, <color=#3366CC>Islam</color> became the
prominent religion and expanded into North Africa. It led to an <color=#3366CC>Islamic Golden Age</color>, inspiring achievements in
<color=#3366CC>architecture</color>, the revival of old advances in science and technology, and the formation of a distinct way of life. The

<color=#3366CC>Christian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Islamic worlds</color> would eventually clash, with the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of England</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of France</color>, and the
<color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color> declaring a series of <color=#3366CC>holy wars</color> to regain control of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Land</color> from <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color>.
In the Americas, between 200 and 900 CE, <color=#3366CC>Mesoamerica</color> was in its Classic Period, while further north, complex
<color=#3366CC>Mississippian societies</color> would arise starting around 800 CE. The <color=#3366CC>Mongol Empire</color> would conquer much of <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> in the
13th and 14th centuries. Over this same time period, the <color=#3366CC>Mali Empire</color> in Africa grew to be the largest empire on the
continent, stretching from Senegambia to <color=#3366CC>Ivory Coast</color>. Oceania would see the rise of the <color=#3366CC>Tui Tonga Empire</color>, which
expanded across many islands in the South Pacific. By the late 15th century, the <color=#3366CC>Aztecs</color> and <color=#3366CC>Inca</color> had become the
dominant power in Mesoamerica and the <color=#3366CC>Andes</color>, respectively.
Modern
The <color=#3366CC>early modern period</color> in Europe and the Near East (c. 1450–1800) began with the <color=#3366CC>final defeat of the Byzantine</color>

<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> and the <color=#3366CC>rise of the Ottoman Empire</color>. Meanwhile, Japan entered the <color=#3366CC>Edo period</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Qing dynasty</color> rose in China,
and the <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color> ruled much of India. Europe underwent the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>, starting in the 15th century, and the
<color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color> began with the exploration and <color=#3366CC>colonization</color> of new regions. This included the <color=#3366CC>colonization of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Americas</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Columbian Exchange</color>. This expansion led to the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic slave trade</color> and the <color=#3366CC>genocide of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Americas' indigenous peoples</color>. This period also marked the <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color>, with great advances in <color=#3366CC>mathematics</color>,
<color=#3366CC>mechanics</color>, <color=#3366CC>astronomy</color>, and <color=#3366CC>physiology</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>late modern period</color> (1800–present) saw the <color=#3366CC>Industrial</color> and <color=#3366CC>Technological Revolution</color> bring such discoveries as
imaging technology, major innovations in transport, and <color=#3366CC>energy development</color>. Influenced by <color=#3366CC>Enlightenment</color> ideals, the
Americas and Europe experienced a period of political revolutions known as the <color=#3366CC>Age of Revolution</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Napoleonic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Wars</color> raged through Europe in the early 1800s, Spain lost most of its colonies in the <color=#3366CC>New World</color>, while Europeans
continued <color=#3366CC>expansion into Africa</color> – where European control went from 10% to almost 90% in less than 50 years – and
Oceania. In the 19th century, the <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color> expanded to become the world's largest empire.
A tenuous <color=#3366CC>balance of power</color> among European nations collapsed in 1914 with the outbreak of the <color=#3366CC>First World War</color>, one
of the deadliest conflicts in history. In the 1930s, <color=#3366CC>a worldwide economic crisis</color> led to the rise of <color=#3366CC>authoritarian</color> regimes
and a <color=#3366CC>Second World War</color>, involving almost all of the world's countries. The war's destruction led to the collapse of most
global empires, leading to widespread decolonization.
Following the conclusion of the Second World War in 1945, the <color=#3366CC>United States</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> emerged as the
remaining <color=#3366CC>global superpowers</color>. This led to a <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color> that saw a struggle for global influence, including a <color=#3366CC>nuclear arms</color>
<color=#3366CC>race</color> and a <color=#3366CC>space race</color>, ending in the collapse of the Soviet Union. The current <color=#3366CC>Information Age</color>, spurred by the
development of the <color=#3366CC>Internet</color> and <color=#3366CC>artificial intelligence</color> systems, sees the world becoming increasingly <color=#3366CC>globalized</color> and
interconnected.
Habitat and population
Early human settlements were dependent on proximity to water and – depending on the lifestyle – other <color=#3366CC>natural</color>
<color=#3366CC>resources</color> used for subsistence, such as populations of animal prey for <color=#3366CC>hunting</color> and <color=#3366CC>arable land</color> for growing crops and
grazing livestock. Modern humans, however, have a great capacity for altering their <color=#3366CC>habitats</color> by means of technology,

<color=#3366CC>irrigation</color>, <color=#3366CC>urban planning</color>, construction, <color=#3366CC>deforestation</color> and <color=#3366CC>desertification</color>. <color=#3366CC>Human settlements</color> continue to be vulnerable
to <color=#3366CC>natural disasters</color>, especially those placed in hazardous locations and with low quality of construction. Grouping and
deliberate habitat alteration are often done with the goals of providing protection, accumulating comforts or material
wealth, expanding the available food, improving <color=#3366CC>aesthetics</color>, increasing knowledge, or enhancing the exchange of
resources.
Humans are one of the most <color=#3366CC>adaptable</color> species, despite having a low or narrow tolerance for many of the Earth's
extreme environments. Currently the species is present in all eight <color=#3366CC>biogeographical realms</color>, although their presence in
the Antarctic realm is limited to research stations, and annually there is a population decline in the winter months of this
realm. Humans have had a dramatic <color=#3366CC>effect on the environment</color>. Human population growth, <color=#3366CC>industrialization</color>, land
development, overconsumption, and combustion of <color=#3366CC>fossil fuels</color> have led to <color=#3366CC>environmental destruction</color> and <color=#3366CC>pollution</color> that
significantly contributes to the ongoing <color=#3366CC>mass extinction</color> of other forms of life.
Within the last century, humans have also explored the deep sea and <color=#3366CC>outer space</color>. Human habitation within these
hostile environments is restrictive and expensive, typically limited in duration, and restricted to <color=#3366CC>scientific</color>, <color=#3366CC>military</color>, or

<color=#3366CC>industrial</color> expeditions. Humans <color=#3366CC>have visited</color> the <color=#3366CC>Moon</color> and made their presence known on other <color=#3366CC>celestial bodies</color>
through human-made <color=#3366CC>robotic spacecraft</color>. Since 2000, there has been continuous human presence in space through
habitation on the <color=#3366CC>International Space Station</color>.
By using advanced tools and <color=#3366CC>clothing</color>, humans have been able to extend their tolerance to a wide variety of
temperatures, <color=#3366CC>humidities</color>, and altitudes. As a result, humans are a cosmopolitan species found in almost all regions of
the world, including <color=#3366CC>tropical rainforests</color>, <color=#3366CC>arid deserts</color>, extremely cold <color=#3366CC>Arctic regions</color>, and heavily polluted cities; in
comparison, most other species are confined to a few geographical areas by their limited adaptability. The human
population is not, however, uniformly distributed on the <color=#3366CC>Earth</color>'s surface, because the population density varies from one
region to another, and large stretches of surface are almost completely uninhabited, like <color=#3366CC>Antarctica</color> and vast swathes of
the ocean. Most humans (61%) live in Asia; the remainder live in the Americas (14%), Africa (14%), Europe (11%), and
Oceania (0.5%).
Estimates of the population at the time agriculture emerged in around 10,000 BC have ranged between 1 million and 15
million. Around 50–60 million people lived in the combined eastern and western <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color> in the 4th century AD.
<color=#3366CC>Bubonic plagues</color>, first recorded in the 6th century AD, reduced the population by 50%, with the <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color> killing
75–200 million people in <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> and <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color> alone. The human population is believed to have reached one billion
in 1800. It has since then increased exponentially, reaching two billion in 1930 and three billion in 1960, four in 1975,
five in 1987, and six billion in 1999. It passed seven billion in 2011 and passed eight billion in 2022. It took over two
million years of <color=#3366CC>human prehistory</color> and <color=#3366CC>history</color> for the human population to reach one billion, and only 207 years more to
grow to 7 billion. The combined biomass of the carbon of all the humans on Earth in 2018 was estimated at 60 million
tons, about 10 times larger than that of all non-domesticated mammals.
In 2018, 4.2 billion humans (55%) lived in urban areas, up from 751 million in 1950. The most urbanized regions are
Northern America (82%), Latin America (81%), Europe (74%), and Oceania (68%), with Africa and Asia having nearly
90% of the world's 3.4 billion rural population. Problems for humans living in cities include various forms of pollution and
<color=#3366CC>crime</color>, especially in inner-city and suburban <color=#3366CC>slums</color>.
Biology
Anatomy and physiology
Most aspects of human physiology are closely <color=#3366CC>homologous</color> to corresponding aspects of animal physiology. The <color=#3366CC>dental</color>
<color=#3366CC>formula</color> of humans is:, like other catarrhines. Humans have proportionately shorter <color=#3366CC>palates</color> and much smaller <color=#3366CC>teeth</color> than
other primates. They are the only primates to have short, relatively flush canine teeth. Humans have characteristically
crowded teeth, with gaps from lost teeth usually closing up quickly in young individuals. Humans are gradually losing
their third molars, with some individuals having them congenitally absent.
Humans share with chimpanzees a <color=#3366CC>vestigial</color> tail, <color=#3366CC>appendix</color>, flexible shoulder joints, grasping fingers and <color=#3366CC>opposable</color>
<color=#3366CC>thumbs</color>. Humans also have a more barrel-shaped chest in contrast to the funnel shape of other apes, an adaptation for
bipedal respiration. Apart from bipedalism and brain size, humans differ from chimpanzees mostly in <color=#3366CC>smelling</color>, <color=#3366CC>hearing</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>digesting proteins</color>. While humans have a density of <color=#3366CC>hair follicles</color> comparable to other apes, it is predominantly
vellus hair, most of which is so short and wispy as to be practically invisible. Humans have about 2 million <color=#3366CC>sweat glands</color>
spread over their entire bodies, many more than chimpanzees, whose sweat glands are scarce and are mainly located
on the palm of the hand and on the soles of the feet.
It is estimated that the worldwide average height for an adult human male is about, while the worldwide average height
for adult human females is about. Shrinkage of stature may begin in middle age in some individuals but tends to be
typical in the extremely <color=#3366CC>aged</color>. Throughout history, human populations have universally become taller, probably as a
consequence of better nutrition, healthcare, and living conditions. The average mass of an adult human is 59 kg for
females and 77 kg for males. Like many other conditions, body weight and body type are influenced by both genetic
susceptibility and environment and vary greatly among individuals.
Humans have a far faster and more accurate throw than other animals. Humans are also among the best long-distance
runners in the animal kingdom, but slower over short distances. Humans' thinner body hair and more productive sweat
glands help avoid heat exhaustion while running for long distances. Compared to other apes, the human <color=#3366CC>heart</color>
produces greater stroke volume and cardiac output, and the <color=#3366CC>aorta</color> is proportionately larger.
Genetics

Humans are, like all animals, <color=#3366CC>plants</color>, and <color=#3366CC>fungi</color>, a <color=#3366CC>eukaryotic</color> species, and like most animals, a <color=#3366CC>diploid</color> species. Each
<color=#3366CC>somatic cell</color> has two sets of 23 <color=#3366CC>chromosomes</color>, each set received from one parent; <color=#3366CC>gametes</color> have only one set of
chromosomes, which is a mixture of the two parental sets. Among the 23 pairs of chromosomes, there are 22 pairs of
autosomes and one pair of <color=#3366CC>sex chromosomes</color>. In humans, sex determination is primarily mediated by the SRY gene
located on the Y chromosome. While the typical configuration follows an XY sex-determination system (XX for females,
XY for males), the genetic expression of the Sex-determining Region Y protein is the critical factor in initiating male
gonadal differentiation. Consequently, individuals may be born with a chromosomal <color=#3366CC>genotype</color> that does not align with
their <color=#3366CC>phenotypic</color> sex, a condition often resulting in infertility due to the absence of specific genes required for
gametogenesis. <color=#3366CC>Genes</color> and <color=#3366CC>environment</color> influence human biological variation in visible characteristics, physiology,
disease susceptibility and mental abilities. The exact influence of genes and environment on certain traits is not well
understood.
While no humans – not even <color=#3366CC>monozygotic twins</color> – are genetically identical, two humans on average will have a genetic
similarity of 99.5%-99.9%. This makes them more homogeneous than other great apes, including chimpanzees. This
small variation in human DNA compared to many other species suggests a <color=#3366CC>population bottleneck</color> during the Late
Pleistocene (around 100,000 years ago), in which the human population was reduced to a small number of breeding
pairs. The forces of <color=#3366CC>natural selection</color> have continued to operate on human populations, with evidence that certain
regions of the <color=#3366CC>genome</color> display directional selection in the past 15,000 years.
In 1984, the US government began to plan the <color=#3366CC>Human Genome Project</color> (HGP), which officially started in 1990. Utilizing
the data from the HGP, 92% of the <color=#3366CC>human genome</color> was first sequenced in 2001. After the HGP was completed in April
2003, the All of Us Research Program in 2022 released its first major dataset, which included nearly 100,000 whole
genome sequences. By April 2023, approximately 245,000 genomes had been sequenced. In 2012, the International
HapMap Project had compared the genomes of 1,184 individuals from 11 populations and identified 1.6 million single
nucleotide polymorphisms. African populations harbor the highest number of private genetic variants. While many of
the common variants found in populations outside of Africa are also found on the African continent, there are still large
numbers that are private to these regions, especially <color=#3366CC>Oceania</color> and <color=#3366CC>the Americas</color>. By 2010 estimates, humans have
approximately 22,000 genes. By comparing <color=#3366CC>mitochondrial DNA</color>, which is inherited only from the mother, geneticists
have concluded that the last female common ancestor whose genetic marker is found in all modern humans, the
so-called <color=#3366CC>mitochondrial Eve</color>, must have lived around 90,000 to 200,000 years ago.
Life cycle
Most <color=#3366CC>human reproduction</color> takes place by internal fertilization via <color=#3366CC>sexual intercourse</color>, but can also occur through
assisted reproductive technology procedures. The average gestation period is 38 weeks, but a normal pregnancy can
vary by up to 37 days. Embryonic development in humans covers the first eight weeks of development; at the beginning
of the ninth week the embryo is termed a <color=#3366CC>fetus</color>. Humans are able to induce early labor or perform a <color=#3366CC>caesarean section</color>
if the child needs to be born earlier for medical reasons. In developed countries, <color=#3366CC>infants</color> are typically 3 – 4 kg in weight
and 47 – 53 cm in height at birth. However, low birth weight is common in developing countries, and it contributes to the
high levels of <color=#3366CC>infant mortality</color> in these regions.
Compared with other species, human childbirth is dangerous, with a much higher risk of complications and death. The
size of the fetus's head is more closely matched to the <color=#3366CC>pelvis</color> than in other primates. The reason for this is not
completely understood, but it contributes to a painful labor that can last 24 hours or more. The chances of a successful
labor increased significantly during the 20th century in wealthier countries with the advent of new medical technologies.
In contrast, pregnancy and natural childbirth remain hazardous ordeals in developing regions of the world, with
maternal death rates approximately 100 times greater than in developed countries.
Both the mother and the father provide care for human offspring, in contrast to other primates, where parental care is
mostly done by the mother. Helpless at birth, humans continue to grow for some years, typically reaching sexual
maturity at 15 to 17 years of age. The human life span has been split into various stages ranging from three to twelve.

Common stages include <color=#3366CC>infancy</color>, <color=#3366CC>childhood</color>, <color=#3366CC>adolescence</color>, <color=#3366CC>adulthood</color> and <color=#3366CC>old age</color>. The lengths of these stages have
varied across cultures and time periods but are typified by an unusually rapid growth spurt during adolescence. Human
females undergo <color=#3366CC>menopause</color> and become <color=#3366CC>infertile</color> at around the age of 50. It has been proposed that menopause
increases a woman's overall reproductive success by allowing her to invest more time and resources in her existing
offspring, and in turn their children (the grandmother hypothesis), rather than by continuing to bear children into old
age.
The life span of an individual depends on two major factors, genetics and lifestyle choices. For various reasons,
including biological/genetic causes, women live on average about four years longer than men. As of 2018, the global
average <color=#3366CC>life expectancy at birth</color> of a girl is estimated to be 74.9 years compared to 70.4 for a boy. There are significant
geographical variations in human life expectancy, mostly correlated with economic development – for example, life
expectancy at birth in <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color> is 87.6 years for girls and 81.8 for boys, while in the <color=#3366CC>Central African Republic</color>, it is
55.0 years for girls and 50.6 for boys. The developed world is generally aging, with the median age around 40 years. In
the <color=#3366CC>developing world</color>, the median age is between 15 and 20 years. While one in five Europeans is 60 years of age or
older, only one in twenty Africans is 60 years of age or older. In 2012, the United Nations estimated that there were
316,600 living centenarians (humans of age 100 or older) worldwide.
Diet
Humans are <color=#3366CC>omnivorous</color>, opportunistic feeders capable of consuming a wide variety of plant and animal material.
Human groups have adopted a range of diets from purely <color=#3366CC>vegan</color> to primarily <color=#3366CC>carnivorous</color>. In some cases, dietary
restrictions in humans can lead to <color=#3366CC>deficiency diseases</color>; however, stable human groups have adapted to many dietary
patterns through both genetic specialization and cultural conventions to use nutritionally balanced food sources. The
human diet is prominently reflected in human culture and has led to the development of <color=#3366CC>food science</color>.
Until the development of agriculture, Homo sapiens employed a hunter-gatherer method as their sole means of food
collection. This involved combining stationary food sources (such as fruits, grains, tubers, and mushrooms, insect
larvae, and aquatic mollusks) with <color=#3366CC>wild game</color>, which must be hunted and captured in order to be consumed. It has been
proposed that humans have used fire to prepare and <color=#3366CC>cook</color> food since the time of <color=#3366CC>Homo erectus</color>. Human <color=#3366CC>domestication</color>
of wild plants began about 11,700 years ago, leading to the <color=#3366CC>development of agriculture</color>, a gradual process called the
<color=#3366CC>Neolithic Revolution</color>. These dietary changes may also have altered human biology; the spread of <color=#3366CC>dairy farming</color>
provided a new and rich source of food, leading to the evolution of the ability to digest <color=#3366CC>lactose</color> in some adults. The
types of food consumed, and how they are prepared, have varied widely by time, location, and culture.
In general, humans can survive for up to eight weeks without food, depending on stored body fat. Survival without
water is usually limited to three or four days, with a maximum of one week. In 2020, it was estimated that 9 million
humans die every year from causes directly or indirectly related to <color=#3366CC>starvation</color>. Childhood malnutrition is also common
and contributes to the global burden of disease. However, global food distribution is not even, and <color=#3366CC>obesity</color> among some
human populations has increased rapidly, leading to health complications and increased mortality in some <color=#3366CC>developed</color>
and a few <color=#3366CC>developing countries</color>. Worldwide, over one billion people are obese, while in the United States, 35% of
people are obese, leading to this being described as an "obesity epidemic." Obesity is caused by consuming more
<color=#3366CC>calories</color> than are expended, so excessive weight gain is usually caused by an energy-dense diet.
Food consumption is the first step of the <color=#3366CC>digestive process</color>, in which humans ultimately expel feces ranging in
frequency from multiple times per day to multiple times per week.
Biological variation
There is biological variation in the human species – with traits such as <color=#3366CC>blood type</color>, <color=#3366CC>genetic diseases</color>, <color=#3366CC>cranial features</color>,

<color=#3366CC>facial features</color>, <color=#3366CC>organ systems</color>, <color=#3366CC>eye color</color>, <color=#3366CC>hair color</color> and <color=#3366CC>texture</color>, height and build, and <color=#3366CC>skin color</color> varying across the
globe. The typical height of an adult human is between 1.4 and 1.9 m, although this varies significantly depending on
sex, <color=#3366CC>ethnic origin</color>, and family bloodlines. Body size is partly determined by genes and is also significantly influenced by
environmental factors such as <color=#3366CC>diet</color>, exercise, and <color=#3366CC>sleep patterns</color>.
There is evidence that populations have adapted genetically to various external factors. The genes that allow adult
humans to digest lactose are present in high frequencies in populations that have long histories of cattle domestication
and are more dependent on <color=#3366CC>cow milk</color>. <color=#3366CC>Sickle cell anemia</color>, which may provide increased resistance to <color=#3366CC>malaria</color>, is
frequent in populations where malaria is endemic. Populations that have for a very long time inhabited specific climates
tend to have developed specific <color=#3366CC>phenotypes</color> that are beneficial for those environments – short stature and stocky build
in cold regions, tall and lanky in hot regions, and with high lung capacities or other adaptations at high altitudes. Some
populations have evolved highly unique adaptations to very specific environmental conditions, such as those
advantageous to ocean-dwelling lifestyles and <color=#3366CC>freediving</color> in the Bajau.
Human hair ranges in color from red to blond to brown to black, which is the most frequent. Hair color depends on the
amount of <color=#3366CC>melanin</color>, with concentrations fading with increased age, leading to grey or even white hair. Skin color can
range from darkest brown to lightest peach, or even nearly white or colorless in cases of <color=#3366CC>albinism</color>. It tends to vary
clinally and generally correlates with the level of <color=#3366CC>ultraviolet radiation</color> in a particular geographic area, with darker skin
mostly around the equator. Skin darkening may have evolved as protection against ultraviolet solar radiation. Light skin
pigmentation protects against depletion of <color=#3366CC>vitamin D</color>, which requires <color=#3366CC>sunlight</color> to make. Human skin also has a capacity
to darken (tan) in response to exposure to ultraviolet radiation.
There is relatively little variation between human geographical populations, and most of the variation that occurs is at
the individual level. Much of human variation is continuous, often with no clear points of demarcation. Genetic data
shows that no matter how population groups are defined, two people from the same population group are almost as
different from each other as two people from any two different population groups. Dark-skinned populations that are
found in Africa, Australia, and South Asia are not closely related to each other.
Genetic research has demonstrated that human populations native to the <color=#3366CC>African continent</color> are the most genetically
diverse and genetic diversity decreases with migratory distance from Africa, possibly the result of <color=#3366CC>bottlenecks</color> during
human migration. These non-African populations acquired new genetic inputs from local <color=#3366CC>admixture with archaic</color>
<color=#3366CC>populations</color> and have much greater variation from Neanderthals and <color=#3366CC>Denisovans</color> than is found in Africa, though
Neanderthal admixture into African populations may be underestimated. Furthermore, recent studies have found that
populations in <color=#3366CC>sub-Saharan Africa</color>, and particularly <color=#3366CC>West Africa</color>, have ancestral genetic variation which predates
modern humans and has been lost in most non-African populations. Some of this ancestry is thought to originate from
admixture with an <color=#3366CC>unknown archaic hominin</color> that diverged before the split of Neanderthals and modern humans.
Humans are a gonochoric species, meaning they are divided into male and female <color=#3366CC>sexes</color>. The greatest degree of
genetic <color=#3366CC>variation exists between males and females</color>. While the nucleotide genetic variation of individuals of the same
sex across global populations is no greater than 0.1%–0.5%, the genetic difference between <color=#3366CC>males</color> and <color=#3366CC>females</color> is
between 1% and 2%. Males on average are 15% heavier and 15 cm taller than females. On average, males have
about 40–50% more upper-body strength and 20–30% more lower-body strength than females at the same weight, due
to higher amounts of muscle and larger muscle fibers. Females generally have a higher <color=#3366CC>body fat</color> percentage than
males. Females have <color=#3366CC>lighter skin</color> than males of the same population; this has been explained by a higher need for
vitamin D in females during pregnancy and <color=#3366CC>lactation</color>. As there are chromosomal differences between females and
males, some X- and Y-chromosome-related conditions and <color=#3366CC>disorders</color> only affect either males or females. After allowing
for body weight and volume, the male voice is usually an octave deeper than the female voice. Females have a <color=#3366CC>longer</color>
<color=#3366CC>life span</color> in almost every population around the world. There are <color=#3366CC>intersex</color> conditions in the human population; however,
these are rare.
Psychology

The <color=#3366CC>human brain</color> is the locus of "higher" order functioning such as <color=#3366CC>thought</color>, <color=#3366CC>reasoning</color>, and <color=#3366CC>abstraction</color>. These <color=#3366CC>cognitive</color>

<color=#3366CC>processes</color> constitute the <color=#3366CC>mind</color>, and, along with their <color=#3366CC>behavioral</color> consequences, are studied in the field of <color=#3366CC>psychology</color>.
Humans have a larger and more developed prefrontal cortex than other primates, the region of the brain associated
with higher <color=#3366CC>cognition</color>. This has led humans to proclaim themselves to be more intelligent than any other known species.
Objectively defining intelligence is difficult, with other animals adapting senses and excelling in areas that humans are
unable to.
There are some traits that, although not strictly unique, do set humans apart from other animals. Humans may be the
only animals who have episodic memory and who can engage in "mental time travel". Even compared with other social
animals, humans have an unusually high degree of flexibility in their facial expressions. Humans are the only animals
known to cry emotional tears. Humans are one of the few animals able to self-recognize in mirror tests, and there is
also debate over to what extent humans are the only animals with a <color=#3366CC>theory of mind</color>.
Sleep and dreaming
Humans are generally diurnal. The average sleep requirement is between seven and nine hours per day for an adult
and nine to ten hours per day for a child; elderly people usually sleep for six to seven hours. Having less sleep than this
is common among humans, even though <color=#3366CC>sleep deprivation</color> can have negative health effects. A sustained restriction of
adult sleep to four hours per day has been shown to correlate with changes in physiology and mental state, including
reduced memory, fatigue, aggression, and bodily discomfort.
During sleep humans dream, where they experience sensory images and sounds. Dreaming is stimulated by the <color=#3366CC>pons</color>
and mostly occurs during the <color=#3366CC>REM phase of sleep</color>. The length of a dream can vary, from a few seconds up to 30
minutes. Humans have three to five dreams per night, and some may have up to seven. Dreamers are more likely to
remember the dream if awakened during the REM phase. The events in dreams are generally outside the control of the
dreamer, with the exception of lucid dreaming, where the dreamer is self-aware. Dreams can at times make a <color=#3366CC>creative</color>
thought occur or give a sense of inspiration, as is the case with some notable works of fiction, scientific concepts, and
art.
Consciousness and thought
Human consciousness, at its simplest, is <color=#3366CC>sentience</color> or awareness of internal or external existence. Despite centuries of
analyses, definitions, explanations and debates by philosophers and scientists, the underlying nature of consciousness
remains enigmatic and poorly understood, being "at once the most familiar and most mysterious aspect of our lives".
The only widely agreed notion about the topic is the intuition that it exists. Opinions differ about what exactly needs to
be studied and explained as consciousness. Some philosophers divide consciousness into phenomenal
consciousness, which is sensory experience itself, and access consciousness, which can be used for reasoning or
directly controlling actions. It is sometimes synonymous with 'the mind', and at other times, an aspect of it. Historically it
is associated with <color=#3366CC>introspection</color>, private <color=#3366CC>thought</color>, <color=#3366CC>imagination</color>, and volition. It now often includes some kind of

<color=#3366CC>experience</color>, <color=#3366CC>cognition</color>, <color=#3366CC>feeling</color> or <color=#3366CC>perception</color>. It may be 'awareness', or 'awareness of awareness', or self-awareness.
There might be different levels or orders of consciousness, or different kinds of consciousness, or just one kind with
different features.
The process of acquiring knowledge and understanding through thought, experience, and the senses is known as
cognition. The human brain <color=#3366CC>perceives</color> the external world through the <color=#3366CC>senses</color>, and each individual human is influenced
greatly by their experiences, leading to subjective views of <color=#3366CC>existence</color> and the passage of time. The nature of thought is
central to psychology and related fields. <color=#3366CC>Cognitive psychology</color> studies <color=#3366CC>cognition</color>, the <color=#3366CC>mental processes</color> underlying
behavior. Largely focusing on the development of the human mind through the life span, <color=#3366CC>developmental psychology</color>
seeks to understand how people come to perceive, understand, and act within the world and how these processes
change as they age. This may focus on intellectual, cognitive, neural, social, or <color=#3366CC>moral development</color>. <color=#3366CC>Psychologists</color> have
developed intelligence tests and the concept of <color=#3366CC>intelligence quotient</color> in order to assess the relative intelligence of
human beings and study its distribution among the population.
Motivation and emotion
Human motivation is not yet wholly understood. From a psychological perspective, Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a
well-established theory that can be defined as the process of satisfying certain needs in ascending order of complexity.
From a more general, philosophical perspective, human motivation can be defined as a commitment to, or withdrawal
from, various goals requiring the application of human ability. Furthermore, incentive and <color=#3366CC>preference</color> are both factors,
as are any perceived links between incentives and preferences. Volition may also be involved, in which case willpower
is also a factor. Ideally, both motivation and volition ensure the selection, striving for, and realization of goals in an
optimal manner, a function beginning in childhood and continuing throughout a lifetime in a process known as
<color=#3366CC>socialization</color>.
Emotions are <color=#3366CC>biological</color> states associated with the nervous system brought on by neurophysiological changes variously
associated with thoughts, feelings, behavioral responses, and a degree of <color=#3366CC>pleasure</color> or <color=#3366CC>displeasure</color>. They are often

intertwined with <color=#3366CC>mood</color>, <color=#3366CC>temperament</color>, <color=#3366CC>personality</color>, disposition, <color=#3366CC>creativity</color>, and motivation. Emotion has a significant
influence on human behavior and their ability to learn. Acting on extreme or uncontrolled emotions can lead to social
disorder and crime, with studies showing criminals may have lower emotional intelligence than normal.
Emotional experiences perceived as <color=#3366CC>pleasant</color>, such as <color=#3366CC>joy</color>, interest, or contentment, contrast with those perceived as

<color=#3366CC>unpleasant</color>, like <color=#3366CC>anxiety</color>, <color=#3366CC>sadness</color>, <color=#3366CC>anger</color>, and <color=#3366CC>despair</color>. <color=#3366CC>Happiness</color>, or the state of being happy, is a human emotional
condition. The definition of happiness is a common philosophical topic. Some define it as experiencing the <color=#3366CC>feeling</color> of
positive emotional affects, while avoiding the negative ones. Others see it as an appraisal of life satisfaction or <color=#3366CC>quality</color>
<color=#3366CC>of life</color>. Recent research suggests that being happy might involve experiencing some negative emotions when humans
feel they are warranted.
Sexuality and love
For humans, sexuality involves <color=#3366CC>biological</color>, erotic, physical, emotional, <color=#3366CC>social</color>, or <color=#3366CC>spiritual</color> feelings and behaviors.
Because it is a broad term that has varied with historical contexts over time, it lacks a precise definition. The biological
and physical aspects of sexuality largely concern the <color=#3366CC>human reproductive functions</color>, including the human sexual
response cycle. Sexuality also affects and is affected by cultural, political, legal, philosophical, <color=#3366CC>moral</color>, <color=#3366CC>ethical</color>, and
religious aspects of life. Sexual desire (<color=#3366CC>libido</color>) is a basic mental state present at the beginning of sexual behavior.
Studies have found that men report stronger sexual desire than women and <color=#3366CC>masturbate</color> more frequently.
Humans can fall anywhere along a continuous scale of <color=#3366CC>sexual orientation</color>, although most humans are <color=#3366CC>heterosexual</color>.
While <color=#3366CC>homosexual</color> behavior occurs in some other animals, only humans and <color=#3366CC>domestic sheep</color> have so far been found to
exhibit exclusive preference for same-sex relationships. Most evidence supports nonsocial, biological causes of sexual
orientation, as cultures that are very tolerant of homosexuality do not have significantly higher rates of it. Research in
<color=#3366CC>neuroscience</color> and <color=#3366CC>genetics</color> suggests that other aspects of human sexuality are biologically influenced as well.
Love most commonly refers to a feeling of strong attraction or emotional <color=#3366CC>attachment</color>. It can be impersonal (the love of
an object, ideal, or strong political or spiritual connection) or interpersonal (love between humans). In the emotional

state of <color=#3366CC>romantic love</color>, neurochemicals such as <color=#3366CC>dopamine</color>, <color=#3366CC>norepinephrine</color>, <color=#3366CC>serotonin</color>, and <color=#3366CC>oxytocin</color> stimulate the brain's
reward system through the mesocorticolimbic pathway (MCL). This dopaminergic pathway may result in side effects

such as <color=#3366CC>tachycardia</color> (increased <color=#3366CC>heart rate</color>), loss of appetite, <color=#3366CC>insomnia</color> (<color=#3366CC>sleeplessness</color>), and <color=#3366CC>intense euphoria</color>.
Culture
Humanity's large set of intellectual skills was a key factor in the species' eventual technological advancement and
concomitant domination of the biosphere. Disregarding extinct hominids, humans are the only animals known to teach
generalizable information, innately deploy recursive embedding to generate and communicate complex concepts,
engage in the "<color=#3366CC>folk physics</color>" required for competent tool design, or cook food in the wild. The ability to preserve and
teach information to future generations in one or more societies is known as the ratchet effect in <color=#3366CC>cultural anthropology</color>.
According to the metaphor, once a group of people understands a technology, it is hard for them to unlearn it, and it
may be used to learn technologies of further complexity. Teaching and learning preserves the cultural and ethnographic
identity of human societies. Other traits and behaviors that are mostly unique to humans include starting fires, <color=#3366CC>phoneme</color>
structuring and vocal learning.
Language
While many species <color=#3366CC>communicate</color>, <color=#3366CC>language</color> is unique to humans, a defining feature of humanity, and a <color=#3366CC>cultural</color>
<color=#3366CC>universal</color>. Unlike the limited communication systems of other animals, human language is open – an infinite number of
meanings can be produced by combining a limited number of symbols. Human language also has the capacity of
displacement, using words to represent things and happenings that are not presently or locally occurring but reside in
the shared imagination of interlocutors.
Language differs from other forms of communication in that it is <color=#3366CC>modality independent</color>; people can convey the same
meanings through different media: audibly in <color=#3366CC>speech</color>, visually by <color=#3366CC>sign language</color> or writing, and through tactile media
such as <color=#3366CC>braille</color>. Language is central to communication between humans, and to the sense of <color=#3366CC>identity</color> that can unite
nations, cultures, and ethnic groups.
As of 1996, humans used approximately six thousand different languages, including sign languages, and many
thousands more are extinct.
The arts

Human arts can take many forms, including <color=#3366CC>visual</color>, <color=#3366CC>literary</color>, and <color=#3366CC>performing</color>. Visual art can range from <color=#3366CC>paintings</color> and

<color=#3366CC>sculptures</color> to <color=#3366CC>film</color>, <color=#3366CC>fashion design</color>, and <color=#3366CC>architecture</color>. Literary arts can include <color=#3366CC>prose</color>, <color=#3366CC>poetry</color>, and <color=#3366CC>dramas</color>. The performing
arts generally involve <color=#3366CC>theater</color>, <color=#3366CC>music</color>, and <color=#3366CC>dance</color>. Humans often combine the different forms (for example, music
videos). Other entities that have been described as having artistic qualities include <color=#3366CC>food preparation</color>, <color=#3366CC>video games</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>medicine</color>. As well as providing entertainment and transferring knowledge, the arts are also used for political purposes.
<color=#3366CC>Art</color> is a defining characteristic of humans, and there is evidence for a relationship between creativity and language. The
earliest evidence of art was shell engravings made by Homo erectus 300,000 years before modern humans evolved.
Art attributed to H. sapiens existed at least 75,000 years ago, with jewelry and drawings found in caves in South Africa.
There are various hypotheses as to why humans have <color=#3366CC>adapted</color> to the arts. These include allowing them to better
problem-solve issues, providing a means to control or influence other humans, encouraging cooperation and
contribution within a society, or increasing the chance of attracting a potential mate. The use of imagination developed
through art, combined with logic, may have given early humans an evolutionary advantage.
Evidence of humans engaging in musical activities predates cave art, and so far music has been <color=#3366CC>practiced by virtually</color>
<color=#3366CC>all known human cultures</color>. There exists a wide variety of <color=#3366CC>music genres</color> and <color=#3366CC>ethnic musics</color>, with humans' musical
abilities being related to other abilities, including complex social human behaviors. It has been shown that human
brains respond to music by becoming synchronized with the rhythm and beat, a process called entrainment. Dance is
also a form of human expression found in all cultures and may have evolved as a way to help early humans
communicate. Listening to music and observing dance stimulates the orbitofrontal cortex and other pleasure-sensing
areas of the brain.
Unlike speaking, reading and writing do not come naturally to humans and must be taught. Still, <color=#3366CC>literature</color> has been
present before the invention of words and language, with 30,000-year-old paintings on walls inside some caves
portraying a series of dramatic scenes. One of the oldest surviving works of literature is the <color=#3366CC>Epic of Gilgamesh</color>, first
engraved on ancient <color=#3366CC>Babylonian</color> tablets about 4,000 years ago. Beyond simply passing down knowledge, the use and
sharing of imaginative <color=#3366CC>fiction</color> through stories might have helped develop humans' capabilities for communication and
increased the likelihood of securing a mate. Storytelling may also be used as a way to provide the audience with moral
lessons and encourage cooperation.
Tools and technologies
Stone tools were used by <color=#3366CC>proto-humans</color> at least 2.5 million years ago. The use and manufacture of tools has been put
forward as the ability that defines humans more than anything else and has historically been seen as an important
evolutionary step. The technology became much more sophisticated about 1.8 million years ago, with the <color=#3366CC>controlled</color>
<color=#3366CC>use of fire</color> beginning around 1 million years ago. The wheel and wheeled vehicles appeared simultaneously in several
regions sometime in the fourth millennium BC. The development of more complex tools and technologies allowed land
to be <color=#3366CC>cultivated</color> and animals to be <color=#3366CC>domesticated</color>, thus proving essential in the development of <color=#3366CC>agriculture</color> – what is
known as the <color=#3366CC>Neolithic Revolution</color>.

<color=#3366CC>China</color> developed <color=#3366CC>paper</color>, the <color=#3366CC>printing press</color>, <color=#3366CC>gunpowder</color>, the <color=#3366CC>compass</color> and other important inventions. The continued

improvements in <color=#3366CC>smelting</color> allowed the <color=#3366CC>forging</color> of copper, bronze, iron, and eventually <color=#3366CC>steel</color>—which is used in <color=#3366CC>railways</color>,
<color=#3366CC>skyscrapers</color>, and many other products. This coincided with the <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>, where the invention of automated
machines brought major changes to humans' lifestyles. Modern technology is observed as progressing exponentially,

with major innovations in the 20th century including: <color=#3366CC>electricity</color>, <color=#3366CC>penicillin</color>, <color=#3366CC>semiconductors</color>, <color=#3366CC>internal combustion engines</color>,

the <color=#3366CC>Internet</color>, <color=#3366CC>nitrogen-fixing fertilizers</color>, <color=#3366CC>airplanes</color>, <color=#3366CC>computers</color>, <color=#3366CC>automobiles</color>, <color=#3366CC>contraceptive pills</color>, <color=#3366CC>nuclear fission</color>, the <color=#3366CC>green</color>

<color=#3366CC>revolution</color>, <color=#3366CC>radio</color>, scientific <color=#3366CC>plant breeding</color>, <color=#3366CC>rockets</color>, <color=#3366CC>air conditioning</color>, <color=#3366CC>television</color> and the <color=#3366CC>assembly line</color>.
Religion and spirituality
Definitions of religion vary; according to one definition, a religion is a <color=#3366CC>belief</color> system concerning the <color=#3366CC>supernatural</color>, <color=#3366CC>sacred</color>

or <color=#3366CC>divine</color>, and practices, <color=#3366CC>values</color>, institutions and <color=#3366CC>rituals</color> associated with such belief. Some religions also have a <color=#3366CC>moral</color>
<color=#3366CC>code</color>. The evolution and the history of the <color=#3366CC>first religions</color> have become areas of active scientific investigation. Credible
evidence of religious behavior dates to the <color=#3366CC>Middle Paleolithic</color> era (45–200 <color=#3366CC>thousand years ago</color>). It may have evolved to
play a role in helping enforce and encourage cooperation between humans.
Religion manifests in diverse forms. Religion can include a belief in <color=#3366CC>life after death</color>, the <color=#3366CC>origin of life</color>, the nature of the

<color=#3366CC>universe</color> (religious cosmology) and its <color=#3366CC>ultimate fate</color> (<color=#3366CC>eschatology</color>), and <color=#3366CC>moral</color> or ethical teachings. Views on

transcendence and immanence vary substantially; traditions variously espouse <color=#3366CC>monism</color>, <color=#3366CC>deism</color>, <color=#3366CC>pantheism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>theism</color>
(including <color=#3366CC>polytheism</color> and <color=#3366CC>monotheism</color>).
Although measuring religiosity is difficult, a majority of humans profess some variety of religious or spiritual belief. In

2015, the plurality was <color=#3366CC>Christian</color>, followed by <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hindu</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Buddhist</color>. As of 2015, about 16%, or slightly under 1.2
billion humans, were <color=#3366CC>irreligious</color>, including those with no religious beliefs or no identity with any religion.
Science and philosophy
A defining attribute of humanity is the capacity for cumulative cultural evolution by transmitting knowledge across
generations by continuously building on past knowledge to develop tools, <color=#3366CC>scientific laws</color>, and other advancements to
pass on to future generations. This accumulated knowledge can be tested to answer various questions or make
predictions about how the universe functions, driving ongoing human advancement. This phenomenon is known as the
ratchet effect in cultural anthropology.
<color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color> has been described as the first scientist, and preceded the rise of scientific thought through the <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic</color>
<color=#3366CC>period</color>. Other early advances in science came from the Han dynasty in China and during the <color=#3366CC>Islamic Golden Age</color>. The
<color=#3366CC>scientific revolution</color>, near the end of the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>, led to the emergence of <color=#3366CC>modern science</color>.
A chain of events and influences led to the development of the <color=#3366CC>scientific method</color>, a process of observation and
experimentation that is used to differentiate science from <color=#3366CC>pseudoscience</color>. An understanding of <color=#3366CC>mathematics</color> is unique
